Fireflies.ai - Transcript

Title: AcmeAI <> Redwood — Route-level A/B testing beta partner sync
Date: 2026-03-05
Time: 09:00 AM PT
Duration: 46 minutes

Attendees
- Simran Kaur (Redwood) — Solutions Architect (Beta partners)
- Marissa Cole (Redwood) — PM, Console & Rollouts
- Logan Wright (Redwood) — Telemetry/Analytics
- Sean Gallagher (Redwood) — SRE (Guardrails)
- Avery Chen (AcmeAI) — Staff ML Engineer
- Maya Patel (AcmeAI) — Platform Engineer
- Jordan Reyes (AcmeAI) — PM, AI features
- Elena Novak (AcmeAI) — SRE

Summary (auto-generated)
- AcmeAI wants to run a route-level A/B on /v1/chat/completions to compare a cheaper quantized variant vs their current baseline model config.
- Primary concern is avoiding latency regressions (TTFT and p95) and avoiding 429s in EU traffic.
- AcmeAI requested clear metric definitions and the ability to export experiment results to their internal dashboards.
- Agreed on a staged rollout plan: start 90/10 in us-east, expand to 50/50 after 24 hours if guardrails are green, then add eu-west with stricter thresholds.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) What AcmeAI is testing and why (cost vs latency)
2) Deterministic assignment key + stickiness expectations
3) Metrics: latency (TTFT/e2e), cost attribution, errors/429s
4) Guardrails, alerts, and rollback workflow
5) Offline eval attachment and quality reporting
6) Rollout schedule + ownership

Questions (auto-generated)
- How does Redwood compute TTFT for streaming responses?
- Can we segment results by region and by customer tier / project?
- What happens if we have retries or reconnects—do we keep the same variant?
- Can we export results, or at least pull via API?

Transcript

[00:00] Simran Kaur: Alright, I think we’re good. Fireflies is recording. Thanks everyone for joining. This is our AcmeAI beta partner sync for the route-level A/B testing feature in Console.

[00:10] Simran Kaur: Quick intros on Redwood side—Simran, solutions architect. Marissa is the product lead for Console and rollouts. Logan from telemetry. Sean from SRE. Do you all want to do quick hellos?

[00:22] Marissa Cole: Hey everyone.

[00:23] Logan Wright: Hi.

[00:24] Sean Gallagher: Morning.

[00:26] Avery Chen: Hey, I’m Avery, ML engineering.

[00:28] Maya Patel: Maya, platform.

[00:29] Jordan Reyes: Jordan, product.

[00:31] Elena Novak: Elena, SRE.

[00:33] Simran Kaur: Cool. Goal today: confirm what you’re trying to test, make sure the metrics and definitions line up with your expectations, and agree on a rollout plan that feels safe.

[00:43] Simran Kaur: Avery, do you want to start with the “what” and “why”?

[00:47] Avery Chen: Yeah. So we’re running… today we’re on your hosted endpoint, same route, /v1/chat/completions. We’re pinned to… I guess you call it a model version? For us it’s basically “baseline” config. We want to compare that against a cheaper variant—quantized weights—and possibly lower max output tokens.

[01:08] Avery Chen: The main driver is cost. We have a feature that’s… it’s basically “draft email + refine.” Lots of streaming. Our concern is TTFT. If TTFT goes up we get user complaints.

[01:21] Jordan Reyes: And just to add, we want to run this in production traffic. Not like an offline sandbox. But we need to be able to stop it quickly if we see latency or error spikes.

[01:33] Simran Kaur: Makes sense. Marissa, anything to add on how the beta is meant to be used?

[01:38] Marissa Cole: That’s exactly the intended use. Route-level experiments are scoped to a route + project, then you can choose variants which are basically (model + config) tuples. And we’re collecting standardized metrics—latency, tokens, cost attribution, errors—plus optionally offline eval deltas.

[01:56] Maya Patel: On that, can you confirm what “config” includes? Like temperature and top_p and max_tokens? Or is it just model revision?

[02:05] Marissa Cole: In the beta: model revision, sampling params like temperature/top_p, max_tokens, and we also support switching some runtime profiles—like different quantization profile if it’s a supported model. We’ll validate allowed fields so you don’t accidentally create an invalid combo.

[02:24] Elena Novak: My main thing is we had a rough week with 429s in EU on a different system. So we’re pretty sensitive to anything that can change routing and load.

[02:35] Sean Gallagher: Yep, that’s why we have guardrails. We can talk thresholds and what triggers alerts / rollback.

[02:41] Simran Kaur: Before guardrails, I want to talk about assignment. Because we had one partner earlier where variant flipping happened due to missing headers.

[02:50] Maya Patel: Yeah, I saw that note you sent. Deterministic assignment is based on hashing some field, right?

[02:56] Marissa Cole: Correct. It’s deterministic bucketing. But it depends on having a stable key. We support a few keys, with precedence. The recommended one is an end-user identifier header (like x-redwood-user-id) if you have it. Otherwise it can fall back to api key id.

[03:14] Avery Chen: We do have a user id internally. We can pass it. But a percentage of calls are system jobs, not tied to a user. Those would not have it.

[03:23] Logan Wright: For those, it would fall back. But if you want absolute stickiness for those too, you can provide a stable “job id” header. The big goal is: whatever key you choose, it must be present consistently. If it’s missing sometimes, you can see flipping across requests.

[03:39] Maya Patel: Okay. So we can do x-acme-user-id maybe, but do you require your own header name?

[03:46] Marissa Cole: We currently allowlist a small set. In beta we’re trying to keep it tight for privacy and cardinality reasons. Simran can send the list. But yes, there is a Redwood header name today.

[04:00] Maya Patel: Got it.

[04:02] Elena Novak: How long does stickiness last? Like if a user comes back tomorrow, do they stay in the same variant?

[04:08] Marissa Cole: It’s deterministic, so as long as the experiment is running with the same bucketing config, they’ll map to the same variant. If you change allocation or add a third arm, obviously the mapping can shift.

[04:22] Elena Novak: Okay.

[04:23] Avery Chen: And retries? We have some client retry logic if the stream reconnects.

[04:27] Marissa Cole: Retries and reconnects should stay consistent. We added that specifically because streaming can be weird—TTFT vs reconnect time. There’s an idempotency key story too, but the primary is the deterministic key.

[04:43] Sean Gallagher: Operationally, if your retry logic changes request headers, that can also break it. So we’ll want to confirm header presence.

[04:52] Simran Kaur: Cool. Let’s move to metrics. Jordan, what metrics do you need to make a go/no-go decision?

[04:59] Jordan Reyes: The big three: p95 latency, and specifically time-to-first-token since we stream; then error rate, including timeouts; and cost. If the cheaper variant is only like 5% cheaper but makes latency 20% worse, that’s a no.

[05:17] Jordan Reyes: Also we want to compare “quality” but honestly we don’t have a perfect online metric.

[05:23] Avery Chen: We can do offline eval. We have a prompt set, and we can do LLM judge maybe, but we have to be careful.

[05:31] Logan Wright: For latency: we record end-to-end gateway latency and TTFT for streaming. TTFT is measured at the gateway from request accepted to first token flushed. For non-stream, it’s basically time-to-first-byte.

[05:47] Maya Patel: Our internal dashboard measures from client side, so that includes network and maybe our proxy.

[05:54] Logan Wright: Yep, so you’ll see differences. The recommended approach is to compare apples to apples—either use Redwood metrics for experiment comparison, or if you export exposures, join with your own client metrics.

[06:07] Maya Patel: Can we export?

[06:09] Marissa Cole: In beta, Console supports CSV export of the summary table. We’re also exposing a results query API internally; public API is not GA yet. But we can work with you. Worst case we can give you a scheduled export for the beta period.

[06:27] Avery Chen: For cost: is it token-based only, or do you do GPU attribution?

[06:31] Logan Wright: Both. We show input tokens, output tokens, total tokens. Cost attribution is token-based in hosted, but we also have internal GPU time attribution that feeds into the cost model. In the UI it’s expressed as “estimated cost per 1k tokens” and “estimated cost per request” for each variant.

[06:52] Jordan Reyes: So it’s not going to match our invoice to the penny.

[06:55] Logan Wright: Correct, it should match at an aggregate level, but we try to make comparisons stable.

[06:59] Elena Novak: Error rate—does that include 429s?

[07:02] Logan Wright: Yes. We break out by status class and include explicit counts for 429, 5xx, and timeouts.

[07:09] Sean Gallagher: And guardrails can be based on those. The beta guardrail evaluator can watch error-rate deltas and latency deltas per variant. We generally suggest: if 429s exceed a threshold OR if p95 latency regression exceeds X% for Y minutes, trigger an alert and optionally auto-rollback.

[07:30] Elena Novak: What’s “X”? Like what do people use?

[07:33] Sean Gallagher: Depends on your baseline. For UI-centric streaming apps, I’d recommend something like: TTFT p95 regression > 15% sustained for 10 minutes is a hard stop. For end-to-end maybe 10–15% as well. Error rate: if 5xx > 0.5% or 429s spike above baseline by, say, +0.2% absolute, that’s often enough to rollback. But we should tune with your actual traffic.

[07:58] Avery Chen: Our baseline TTFT p95 is around 900ms in us-east and 1.2s in eu-west. We can tolerate like… maybe +150ms? We can’t tolerate +500ms.

[08:12] Sean Gallagher: That’s helpful. We can translate that into a percent threshold.

[08:16] Marissa Cole: We also show confidence indicators, but I want to caveat: in early hours, you’ll have low sample sizes, so we try not to overstate significance.

[08:27] Avery Chen: Yeah, we get it.

[08:29] Simran Kaur: On quality: you mentioned offline eval. What would you like to see in Console?

[08:35] Avery Chen: Mostly: pass/fail on some rubric. Like “does it follow instructions,” “does it include sensitive content,” “did it hallucinate pricing.” We can do a judge model with a structured rubric.

[08:50] Jordan Reyes: I’d like to show stakeholders a simple “quality delta” chart. Not too academic.

[08:56] Marissa Cole: In v1, we can attach an eval suite and show aggregate score and delta between variants, plus confidence intervals. We also include a warning when sample size is low.

[09:10] Avery Chen: Great.

[09:12] Maya Patel: One thing: if we run the experiment at route-level, can we scope by region? Like only us-east first.

[09:19] Marissa Cole: Yes, region eligibility is supported. You can start us-east only.

[09:23] Elena Novak: Please do that.

[09:26] Simran Kaur: Let’s propose a rollout plan and see if it works.

[09:30] Simran Kaur: Phase 1: 90/10 in us-east only, baseline as control, cheaper quantized as treatment. Run for 24 hours. Watch TTFT p95, end-to-end p95, 429, 5xx.

[09:44] Simran Kaur: Phase 2: if guardrails are green and you’re happy with quality in offline eval snapshot, move to 50/50 us-east for another day.

[09:54] Simran Kaur: Phase 3: add eu-west at 90/10 first with stricter thresholds.

[10:02] Jordan Reyes: That works.

[10:03] Elena Novak: I like the EU being last. Also want an “oh no” button.

[10:08] Sean Gallagher: There is an emergency disable. It sets the experiment state to “disabled” and routes 100% to control. We also have a rollback workflow that logs an audit event.

[10:20] Maya Patel: Is it instant?

[10:22] Sean Gallagher: Within a minute or two depending on config propagation. For hosted it’s usually under 60 seconds.

[10:30] Avery Chen: Can we do it ourselves or do we page you?

[10:33] Marissa Cole: You can do it in Console, assuming you have permissions. Which brings up RBAC.

[10:38] Jordan Reyes: Yeah, permissions. We want only platform folks to be able to start/stop.

[10:44] Marissa Cole: In beta, it’s behind an entitlement plus role checks. You can restrict it to Admin/Owner roles. We also show an audit log view—who changed allocations, who started it, who stopped it.

[10:59] Elena Novak: Audit logs—can we send to our SIEM?

[11:02] Marissa Cole: Not in v1 beta. But we can export audit events if needed for the beta. GA will have more.

[11:09] Simran Kaur: I can coordinate if you need an export. For now, at least you’ll have the in-Console audit trail.

[11:17] Maya Patel: Another question: overlap with canaries. We also use your canary rollout sometimes.

[11:22] Marissa Cole: Great question. The precedence is: reliability fallbacks first, then experiments. So if there’s a fallback triggered, it can override an experiment assignment. That’s intentional to keep the service up.

[11:35] Avery Chen: That could mess up the experiment results, right?

[11:38] Logan Wright: We log exposures and also log when a fallback happened. In reporting we can filter out fallback-affected requests or at least annotate. But yes, if you’re falling back a lot, your experiment isn’t clean.

[11:54] Sean Gallagher: And if you’re falling back a lot, you probably want to stop anyway.

[11:58] Elena Novak: Fair.

[12:01] Jordan Reyes: For this test, we’re not planning canaries on top of it. So fine.

[12:06] Simran Kaur: Let’s talk about the actual variant configs. Avery, what are you thinking for treatment?

[12:12] Avery Chen: Baseline is your “Redwood verified” model, temperature 0.2, max_tokens 512. Treatment: same model family but quantized, and max_tokens 384. Maybe slightly higher temperature, but we can keep it same.

[12:30] Marissa Cole: I’d strongly recommend keeping sampling the same in the first run, otherwise you’ll be attributing quality shifts to multiple variables.

[12:38] Avery Chen: Yep, agreed.

[12:41] Maya Patel: What about prompt changes? We might tweak prompts during the experiment.

[12:45] Marissa Cole: Please don’t, if you can avoid. If you have to, we should note it and maybe restart.

[12:52] Jordan Reyes: We can freeze prompts for a week.

[12:55] Simran Kaur: Perfect.

[12:57] Logan Wright: One more metric note: token counts can change with max_tokens changes. So your cost delta might be partly “we cut outputs short,” not purely runtime cost. That’s fine, but interpret accordingly.

[13:12] Avery Chen: Right, but that’s part of the point. We want to see if users notice.

[13:17] Jordan Reyes: Exactly. Product-wise we’re okay with slightly shorter output if it’s still useful.

[13:23] Simran Kaur: On exposures: do you need segmenting by plan tier or something?

[13:27] Maya Patel: We have multiple projects in Redwood. We only want this for one project.

[13:31] Marissa Cole: That’s supported. It’s scoped to a project and route.

[13:35] Elena Novak: And by region is a must.

[13:37] Logan Wright: Region filtering is in the dashboard.

[13:41] Avery Chen: Could we segment by customer “workspace”? Like multi-tenant on our side.

[13:46] Logan Wright: Not directly. We avoid high-cardinality dimensions in the core metrics. But you can choose the bucketing key such that it’s stable per workspace if that’s what you want. For analysis, you could join your own logs using the exposure id, but we don’t expose a raw identifier that ties back to a tenant. Privacy reasons.

[14:08] Avery Chen: Understood.

[14:10] Jordan Reyes: Okay, so basically the Console dashboard is for overall comparison, not deep per-tenant slicing.

[14:16] Marissa Cole: Correct.

[14:18] Elena Novak: On alerts: do we get paged or do you get paged?

[14:22] Sean Gallagher: In beta, Redwood gets paged for platform issues. For your experiment guardrails, we can route alerts to your email/Slack channel if you want, but the simplest is: you watch the dashboard and we also watch, and if there’s a regression we ping you. GA will have more self-serve alert routing.

[14:41] Elena Novak: We prefer something that hits our on-call Slack.

[14:44] Sean Gallagher: We can do that via an integration on our side for the beta. Simran can coordinate.

[14:50] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[14:52] Maya Patel: I have a question about 429s specifically. If treatment is slower, could it trigger more 429s because it consumes capacity longer?

[15:01] Sean Gallagher: Potentially. If the treatment variant has lower throughput, it can increase queueing. That’s why we start at 10% and why we use region gating.

[15:10] Logan Wright: Also, we track concurrency and queue time internally. Not all of that is exposed in v1 UI, but we can look if we see weirdness.

[15:22] Avery Chen: Can the experiment route more than 10% by accident? Like mis-bucketing.

[15:27] Marissa Cole: It shouldn’t. We’ve had bugs in early builds, but in the current beta build the bucketing is fixed and validated. Also we have a “traffic observed vs configured” widget to catch drift.

[15:40] Maya Patel: Nice. That’s actually very useful.

[15:43] Simran Kaur: Let’s lock down schedule. When do you want to start?

[15:48] Jordan Reyes: Ideally next Tuesday. We have a release Monday.

[15:53] Elena Novak: Tuesday morning Pacific is okay. That gives us business hours coverage.

[15:59] Simran Kaur: Great. We can enable the flag in your project by end of this week, then you can set up the experiment but keep it paused.

[16:08] Maya Patel: There’s a “paused” state?

[16:10] Marissa Cole: Yes. Draft, validated, paused, running, stopped. Draft is editable. Running locks some fields. Paused is basically “configured but not routing.”

[16:23] Jordan Reyes: We want that.

[16:25] Avery Chen: And we can name variants “control” and “treatment” or like “A” and “B”?

[16:30] Marissa Cole: You can label them, but we recommend “Control” and “Challenger” to reduce confusion. We’ve seen customers label “B” as baseline and it gets messy.

[16:42] Jordan Reyes: We’ll do Control/Challenger.

[16:45] Maya Patel: Okay.

[16:47] Logan Wright: When you attach the offline eval, it’ll run against both variants and produce a report. For sample size: if you can provide 200-ish prompts, that’s a good starting point.

[16:58] Avery Chen: We can do 250.

[17:01] Logan Wright: Perfect.

[17:03] Simran Kaur: Any other concerns?

[17:06] Elena Novak: I want a clear runbook. Like if we see 429 spike, what steps, what to check.

[17:12] Sean Gallagher: We have one. It’s basically: disable experiment, verify traffic returns to control, check error rates normalize, then we can dig into root cause—capacity, misconfig, or treatment throughput. I’ll send you the steps.

[17:28] Maya Patel: For verifying it’s disabled—do we have a log or something?

[17:33] Logan Wright: You can see exposure volume per variant. If it drops to zero for challenger, you’re good. Also audit event shows “experiment disabled by X.”

[17:44] Jordan Reyes: Great.

[17:46] Avery Chen: One last thing: we might want to keep the cheaper model for some percentage even after the experiment if it looks good. Is there a “graduate” path?

[17:56] Marissa Cole: Yes. At the end you can either stop and then update your route to pin to the winner, or convert it into a rollout policy. We’re still smoothing that UX, but operationally it’s straightforward.

[18:10] Simran Kaur: Cool. Let’s do a recap and next steps.

[18:13] Simran Kaur: Recap: You’ll run /v1/chat/completions experiment in one project. Control is current pinned model config. Challenger is quantized variant with same sampling, and likely reduced max_tokens.

[18:27] Simran Kaur: Rollout: start Tuesday in us-east at 90/10 for 24h, then 50/50 if green, then eu-west 90/10.

[18:37] Simran Kaur: Guardrails: we’ll propose TTFT p95 threshold around +15% or +150ms-ish for you, plus strict monitoring of 429 and 5xx. Sean will send recommended numbers.

[18:50] Simran Kaur: Action items: I’ll send the header requirements and enablement checklist. Maya will confirm which stable identifier header you can pass consistently and coverage. Avery will send offline eval prompt set. Logan will share metric definitions so you can compare to your dashboards.

[19:06] Jordan Reyes: Sounds good.

[19:08] Elena Novak: Yep.

[19:10] Avery Chen: Thanks.

[19:12] Simran Kaur: Great. We’ll follow up over email today or tomorrow. Appreciate it.

[19:17] (call ends)

Notes
- Some crosstalk and minor transcription errors present; speaker attribution may be imperfect in a few spots.
- References: Redwood Console (Experiments), route-level A/B testing beta, exposure logging, TTFT definitions, guardrail rollback runbook.
